title: Finding The Next Perfect Trade | Alex Gurevich
analysis: ### Executive Summary The speaker, Alex Gurovich, a veteran global macro trader and author, provides a strategic framework for investment rather than specific market predictions. He emphasizes adapting to changing market regimes, particularly the shift from a low-inflation, low-rate environment (post-2008) to the current higher inflation and rates. His core market outlook is fundamentally contrarian: he foresees a new bull market in US Treasuries, predicting that front-end rates will eventually fall back to zero due to a disinflationary spiral driven by deteriorating job markets amidst high real rates. He acknowledges the current strength of the stock market but believes it will eventually become "much cheaper." Gurovich also highlights the profound, unpredictable impact of AI/AGI, which he believes is arriving on schedule, displacing human labor and discretionary trading. He advises investors to position portfolios with intrinsic value today, as AI-driven capital will eventually converge on these assets. He advocates for simple, long-term trade expressions, using options primarily for portfolio-level risk management, and prioritizing trades that work "now or later" while maintaining flexibility to exit trades when conviction wanes. He admits a lack of fundamental understanding for some asset movements (like precious metals) but acknowledges their momentum-driven performance. ### Asset Breakdown #### AI / AGI / Singularity Sentiment: Bullish (+0.9) Thesis: AI (Artificial General Intelligence) is arriving, slightly faster than anticipated. This will lead to a fundamental transformation of global macroeconomics and labor markets. While potentially leading to an overall positive growth on a very large scale, it will also eliminate entire areas of human economic activity, causing deflationary pressure and job redundancy. It will eventually displace discretionary human trading. Key Levels: Not mentioned. Risks: The precise impact is "very hard to predict" and human minds may lack the capacity to fully comprehend its implications. Potential for "anti-growth component" in specific areas due to job elimination. Catalysts: AlphaGo (2016) was a turning point. The current rapid advancement of AI technologies. Quote: "I laugh at people who have people who who express any kind of skepticism of about the power of AI." #### Stock Market (US Equities) Sentiment: Bearish (-0.7) Thesis: While currently "nothing bearish you can say about the stock market" and it "could go up under any circumstances," history shows that "at some point, things run out of steam and start going down." The speaker's "kind of bet is that something will happen and stock market at some point will be much cheaper." This will be driven by a dwindling financial impulse from the stock market itself. Key Levels: Not mentioned. Risks: The market has shown an ability to continue rallying despite headwinds. It is difficult to predict *when* a downturn will occur. Catalysts: A "dwindling financial impulse" from the stock market combined with "decaying job markets." No specific timeframe, but "at some point." Quote: "My kind of bet is that something will happen and stock market at some point will be much cheaper." #### US Rates / Treasuries Sentiment: Bullish (+0.8) Thesis: It's "time for the new bull market in treasuries." The combination of relatively high US rates and a deteriorating job market suggests a "disinflationary spiral." The market is not currently pricing this scenario, creating a "disproportionate chance for the rates to go back down to zero on the front end in US." The Fed, being "burnt by inflation," is reluctant to cut rates rapidly, and the curve is resisting cuts, which paradoxically makes disinflation more likely as policy response will be behind the curve. Key Levels: Rates going "back down to zero on the front end." Risks: The Fed's reluctance to cut rates rapidly due to inflation fears. The market is "stuck on the idea of inflation." Lagging inflationary and job market numbers mean the true state of disinflation may not be known for a "very long time." Catalysts: Deterioration of the job market; an environment of positive real rates. Quote: "I think there's disproportionate chance for the rates to go back down to zero on the front end in US." #### Bonds (Secular Trend) Sentiment: Bearish (-0.9) on the *past* secular trend, Neutral (0.0) on *future* general bond performance (context-dependent). Thesis: The "one chart that rules them all" – the 30-year uptrend in bonds (roll-adjusted bond futures) – "definitely broke down" in 2020-2022. The speaker admits a significant mistake in not recognizing this breakdown, having previously believed that slow grinds up always end in parabolic rallies before breaking down. The COVID rally's break *up* should have signaled a potential subsequent breakdown. Key Levels: Not mentioned. Risks: Not recognizing major regime shifts or breakdowns in long-term trends. Catalysts: The COVID rally in 2020 which saw bonds break their trading channel on the way up, signaling a potential reversal. Quote: "I made a big mistake not recognizing the breakdown on this chart." #### Risk Parity Paradigm Sentiment: Bearish (-0.9) Thesis: The "risk parity paradigm" (the idea that if stocks go down, bonds go up, or vice versa, allowing investors to be long both) experienced a "big breakdown" in 2022. During this period, both the stock market and the bond market sold off simultaneously, leading to "sell America moments." This historical correlation no longer reliably holds. Key Levels: Not mentioned. Risks: Relying on outdated or broken market paradigms. Catalysts: The market behavior in 2022, where both asset classes declined. Quote: "in like 2022 we had a big breakdown of this risk parity paradigm." #### Dollar (USD) Sentiment: Mixed (0.0) Thesis: The dollar's direction depends on liquidity conditions. If liquidity is low and real rates are high, it might be a good trade to be "long dollar against some currencies with all low yields like China, Hong Kong, Taiwan." However, in "sell America moments" (where equities, bonds, and dollar all fall), the dollar can go lower. Key Levels: Not mentioned. Risks: The US market environment is "a little more confusing right now" with many crosscurrents, making it hard to predict the dollar's behavior with certainty. Catalysts: Low global liquidity (bullish USD); "Sell America" conditions (bearish USD). Quote: "Will dollar will dollar have to like for example the market projects rates to stay high and actually grind up in the next few years. Is it positive for the dollar or negative for the dollar and so on?" #### Yen (JPY) Sentiment: Bullish (+0.7) (on future rally) Thesis: While the speaker "did not catch the yen trade" (implying missing its depreciation), a Yen rally is now a "concurrent necessity" in the event of a failure of long-dated Japanese bond trades. Specifically, if the Bank of Japan (BOJ) were to raise short-term rates to 4%, a stronger Yen would likely follow, as it would stabilize the long end of the yield curve, especially if other countries are cutting rates. Key Levels: Not mentioned. Risks: Inflation spinning out of control to the point where BOJ raises rates significantly, but Yen still fails to rally. Non-market actors like the Ministry of Finance intervening in the short run could introduce chaos, though over several years, their actions become more predictable (they would eventually intervene to stop a currency slide if it went "too far"). Catalysts: BOJ raising short-term rates significantly (e.g., to 4%). Other countries continuing to cut rates. Quote: "I think yen will rally a lot so paradoxically yen rally is a concurrent necessity with respect to lo failure of the long bond trade in in in in Japan." #### Japanese Government Bonds (JGBs) (Long-dated) Sentiment: Bullish (+0.7) Thesis: Long-dated Japanese bonds are "beginning to look attractive" at a 4% yield. Japan currently has extremely low real rates, very low front-end rates, a weak currency, high inflation, and a "very steep yield curve." Buying these bonds offers positive carry for as long as short-term rates remain below 4%. Key Levels: Buying at 4% yield. Risks: Japan defaulting (dismissed as very low probability due to no external debt and government ownership of most debt). The primary risk for this trade failing is short-term rates rising to 4% or higher, which would eliminate the positive carry. Catalysts: The current market conditions of low short-term rates, high inflation, and steep yield curve make the long end attractive. Quote: "longan in Japan is bond market is beginning to look attractive." #### Precious Metals (Gold, Silver) Sentiment: Bullish (+0.8) Thesis: When liquidity is high, "precious metals will just be running." Sometimes, "you just have to kind of like give up and just run with the market," especially when "location" (historical charts/typical ranges) might not be ideal, but the "stories" (narratives) are still supportive. The rally might be driven by speculative money, strategic buying, or even AI algorithms calculating higher fair values. Key Levels: Silver historical ranges: $20, $60 (neutral), $115 ("not a good location"). Gold: speculative target of $10,000 (AI-driven). Risks: The speaker admits, "I don't really know what drives silver to $115 an ounce or whatever it is... there is no mathematical formula which says that silver should be $20 an ounce, $60 an ounce, or $110 an ounce." Assets can "run out of steam." Catalysts: High liquidity conditions. Market momentum. Potential AI buying. Quote: "Sometimes sometimes you just have to kind of like give up and just run with the market." #### Copper Sentiment: Bullish (+0.6) (long-term); Neutral (short-term) Thesis: "Long copper is probably a good trade" under strong global growth conditions. Even if global growth is stunted in the short term, copper will likely remain in demand in the long term due to increasing electricity demands globally, making it a "will work now or will work later" trade. Key Levels: Not mentioned. Risks: Short-term gyrations due to factors like tariffs. Global growth being stunted could negatively impact performance in the short horizon. Catalysts: Strong global growth (short-term); increasing global demand for electricity (long-term). Quote: "Probably copper will stay in demand, right? So under this under this condition, I was like, okay, uh you can belong copper." #### Oil Sentiment: Bearish (-0.3) Thesis: In previous years, oil offered "very good positive carry" due to backwardation (deferred oil cheaper than spot). However, "in 2025, oil just starts grinding down and I gave up on it and got out." The carry trade stopped working as contracts closed and oil entered a downtrend. Key Levels: Not mentioned. Risks: Downtrend in price can negate positive carry benefits. Catalysts: Positive carry from backwardation (historically, now past). Quote: "in 2025, oil just starts grinding down and I gave up on it and got out." #### Crypto (Bitcoin, Ethereum, Digital Asset Space) Sentiment: Bullish (+0.5) Thesis: Crypto is positioned as an asset class that benefits from high liquidity conditions, alongside precious metals. It's an option for "whatever you think is cheapest on the charts on like historical rangers and try to run that to what will run on high liquidity." Key Levels: Not mentioned. Risks: General investment risks including "possible loss of principle." Catalysts: High liquidity in the market. Quote: "If liquidity is high probably precious metals will just be running. So you look at whatever precious metals or you can choose like between crypto precious industrial." ### Critique The speaker, Alex Gurovich, offers a sophisticated and self-aware approach to macro trading. His logic is generally sound, rooted in strategic thinking developed over decades. **Strengths:** * **Self-Correction and Learning from Mistakes:** Gurovich openly acknowledges his "big mistake" in not fully internalizing the breakdown of the secular bond bull market, demonstrating intellectual honesty and adaptability, which is crucial for long-term success. * **Contrarian Thinking:** His high-conviction view that US rates will fall to zero, despite current inflation fears, is a well-articulated contrarian thesis backed by a concurrent necessity framework (deteriorating job market + high real rates = disinflation). * **Focus on Strategic Principles:** He rightly emphasizes what makes a *good trade* (ex-ante characteristics) rather than just predicting market direction, which aligns with robust portfolio management. * **Realistic View on AI:** His long-term perspective on AI's disruptive potential, including its impact on labor and discretionary trading, provides a valuable and sobering outlook. He is also pragmatic about how to leverage it or align with its potential influence on markets. * **Nuanced Risk Management:** His opposition to blanket mechanical stop-losses and preference for options as portfolio risk management tools (especially when views are highly confident but could be catastrophically wrong) highlights a deep understanding of risk beyond simple thresholds. **Areas for Further Consideration/Critique:** * **Subjectivity of "Giving Up":** While understandable that traders sometimes "just run with the market" or "give up on a trade," the decision to exit a position "because it didn't feel really good anymore to me" can be subjective and prone to emotional biases, even for experienced traders. He does mention "other reasons" to get out, but these are not explicitly detailed. * **Lack of Fundamental Valuation for Precious Metals:** He candidly admits, "I really don't know what drives silver to $115 an ounce or whatever it is." While his strategy to "run with the market" during momentum phases is valid, it highlights a reliance on technicals and market psychology without underlying fundamental support, which can be risky for longer-term positions if momentum shifts abruptly. * **General Lack of Specific Price Targets/Key Levels:** Apart from the 4% yield for JGBs and a speculative $10,000 for gold (AI-driven), specific entry, stop-loss, or take-profit levels are largely absent. This aligns with his preference for strategic, longer-term views and less mechanical trading but makes direct "actionable intelligence" in terms of entry/exit points less concrete for immediate application. **Critique Mentioned by the Speaker:** * **His own mistake:** Not fully internalizing the breakdown of the secular bull bond market after it had a parabolic rally in 2020. * **Skepticism about AI:** He views skepticism about AI's power as "laughable," having foreseen its transformative impact since 2016.

title: Bitcoin: Bear Market Resistance Band
analysis: ### Executive Summary The speaker, a crypto analyst, presents a strongly bearish outlook for Bitcoin (BTC) and altcoins, predicting a prolonged bear market extending into summer 2026. He characterizes the current market as one of "slightly lower lows and slightly lower highs," drawing parallels to past midterm election years (2014, 2018, 2022) and the "apathy" phase observed in 2019. He asserts that the "bull market support band" has now transitioned into the "bear market resistance band." The analyst forecasts a significant 50% drop from recent highs for Bitcoin and expects it to sweep prior lows, specifically mentioning a target around the "low from April of 2025." Conversely, he expresses a bullish sentiment for "harder assets" such as gold and silver, attributing their strength to ongoing fiat money printing and the declining purchasing power of the US Dollar, advocating for asset valuation against these commodities. Altcoins are deemed a poor short-term investment given Bitcoin's bearish trend. ### Asset Breakdown #### Bitcoin (BTC) Thesis: The speaker believes Bitcoin is in a clear bear market, evidenced by historical cycle lengths (1,062 days for the past cycle, consistent with previous cycles of 1,059 and 1,068 days) and recurring patterns in midterm years (2014, 2018, 2022). He observes "slightly lower lows and slightly lower highs," comparing the current trajectory to the 2019 market top characterized by apathy. The previously identified "bull market support band" has now flipped to become the "bare market resistance band," suggesting resistance on upward moves. He also notes Bitcoin's underperformance against gold and silver as further evidence of its bear market status. Key Levels: Expected "50% drop from the highs" in 2026. Anticipates a "sweep of the prior low," specifically targeting "the low from April of 2025." The trend is expected to be "slightly lower lows and slightly lower highs going into the summer of 2026." Risks: The speaker acknowledges that "some people might look at this and say well you know could it be doing the same thing that it did previously where it kind of goes up there and isn't really able to get through on the first attempt. It's possible." However, he quickly dismisses this, reinforcing his bearish stance. Sentiment: Bearish (-0.9) Quote: "My guess is that it's just going to continue this path of slightly lower lows and slightly lower highs going into the summer of 2026. And until proven otherwise, the bull market support band is the bare market resistance band." #### Altcoins Thesis: The speaker asserts that altcoins are generally not a good investment, especially when Bitcoin is in a bear market. He believes that while "some alts can't go up," "most of them likely will drop." He emphasizes the importance of valuing altcoins against Bitcoin rather than just US dollars. Key Levels: Not considered a good investment "in the short term." Risks: The speaker does not explicitly mention risks to his bearish altcoin thesis but notes that "there's a lot of people calling for for different things and and saying that altcoins will rally." Sentiment: Bearish (-0.9) Quote: "I've sort of repeated myself over and over and over again how altcoins are not a good investment in my opinion... I just don't think they have been. Um, and I I don't think they will be in the short term either." #### Metals (Gold, Silver) Thesis: The speaker is bullish on metals, stating that "metals are going up" and highlighting a "shift to harder assets" away from altcoins. He suggests valuing assets against gold due to the continuous printing of US dollars and the perceived decline in the dollar's purchasing power. Key Levels: "Gold's above 5,000, silver's above 100." (These are presented as statements of current strong performance or projected future valuation by the speaker rather than traditional entry/exit points.) Risks: No specific risks to the bullish thesis for metals were mentioned. Sentiment: Bullish (0.8) Quote: "We have a market where metals are going up. Gold's above 5,000, silver's above 100. We have a shift to harder assets, right? Away from altcoins and towards harder assets." #### US Dollar (USD) / Fiat Currency Thesis: The speaker holds a highly bearish view on the US Dollar, stating that its "purchasing power... is going as to zero." This is attributed to the continuous "printing money" by authorities, making it an unreliable measure for asset valuation. Key Levels: Its purchasing power is "going as to zero." Risks: No specific risks to the bearish thesis for the US Dollar were mentioned. Sentiment: Bearish (-0.9) Quote: "This is why you don't want to measure things typically in US dollars because they're never going to stop printing money and the persing power of the US dollar as we know is going as to zero." ### Critique The speaker's logic relies heavily on historical cyclical analysis for Bitcoin, specifically focusing on cycle length and performance during midterm election years. While historical patterns can be informative, assuming direct repetition without accounting for evolving market structures, institutional adoption, or broader macroeconomic shifts (beyond just money printing) introduces an element of risk. The assertion that the "bull market support band" is now the "bear market resistance band" is a valid technical observation, but its predictive power is context-dependent. The speaker dismisses alternative bullish perspectives for Bitcoin and altcoins quite rapidly, providing limited deep-dive arguments against them, which could be seen as a confirmation bias towards his existing bearish view. He correctly highlights the importance of valuing assets against more stable stores of value like gold, especially given inflationary concerns, and the comparative performance of Bitcoin against gold and silver provides a valuable alternative perspective to USD-denominated charts. A significant point of critique lies in the "Key Levels" mentioned for metals: "Gold's above 5,000, silver's above 100." These figures are substantially higher than current market prices for these commodities and are presented by the speaker as if they are current realities or easily achievable levels, without further clarification if they are a future projection, a relative valuation against specific fiat, or a rhetorical exaggeration. This could be misleading for investors looking for actionable price targets. The specific Bitcoin target of "the low from April of 2025" is also a future projection that lacks detailed fundamental or technical justification beyond the general "sweep of prior lows" concept. The speaker's own critique of the market is that "a lot of people would love for Bitcoin to be at a bull market" and "for all season," but he stresses the importance of "trade the market that you have, not the market that you want." He also acknowledges that his views "are not the best views for people that want to see Bitcoin go up," implying he recognizes the unpopularity of his bearish stance among certain market participants.

title: Two Important Charts For Gold!
analysis: ### Executive Summary The speaker, a Senior Investment Analyst and Portfolio Manager with a long-standing bullish view on gold, reaffirms his conviction, citing gold's recent attainment of new all-time highs. The primary investment thesis for gold is anchored on its strong performance relative to the S&P 500, with the latter showing significant underperformance when valued against gold. Additionally, the gold-to-money-supply (M2) ratio has decisively broken past critical historical resistance levels, signaling further upside potential. The speaker forecasts a target of over $6,000 for gold, aligning with a long-term projection made years prior, driven by macro landscape shifts and an anticipated continuation of a breakout, backtest, and subsequent rally pattern observed in other assets. He suggests investors should favor gold over currently "bearish" crypto markets and the "bleeding" stock market, despite acknowledging potential short-term pullbacks. ### Asset Breakdown #### Gold Thesis: Gold is breaking out against the S&P 500, meaning the S&P is significantly underperforming gold (down almost 50% against gold since January 2022, despite being up 44% in USD terms). The gold/M2 ratio has taken out highs from 2011, indicating significant room for further appreciation. This pattern of breakout, backtest, and run higher has been observed in Bitcoin dominance, the HSI, and Palladium. The current macroeconomic environment, where the Fed is not printing money in the same way as 2020, supports gold's ascent. It is presented as a superior investment choice compared to crypto (seen as in a bear market) and the stock market (bleeding against gold). Key Levels: Current price is around 5180 (likely referring to the gold/M2 ratio or an implicit USD price near $2400-2500, but 5180 mentioned with relation to a 20% rally). A 20% rally from current levels would put gold "right above $6,000." This $6,000 target aligns with a projection made 5-6 years ago and is potentially a "sweep of the high that it had in August, September 1982" on the gold/M2 chart. Risks: A potential for a short-term correction on its USD pair. Expectation of a pullback against the stock market before it goes higher. There might be a stalling out around the $6,000 mark before another run. Sentiment: Bullish (Confidence: 1) Quote: "Gold is breaking out against the S&P or you can view it as the stock market is breaking down against gold. It doesn't really matter how you view it. That's just the way it goes." #### S&P 500 Thesis: The S&P 500 is breaking down significantly against gold. Since January 2022, despite a 44% rise in USD terms, the S&P is down almost 50% against gold. This indicates a long-term shift where the stock market is "just bleeding to gold." Key Levels: Not specified, as the discussion is about relative performance rather than absolute price targets. Risks: While short-term mean reversion might occur, it's not considered a long-term bullish trade opportunity against gold. Sentiment: Bearish (relative to Gold) (Confidence: -0.8) Quote: "Despite the fact that the S&P has gone up 40%. The S&P is down almost 50% against gold over that period of time. That might seem weird to a lot of people." #### Crypto (General) Thesis: Crypto appears to be in a bear market currently. The speaker is not placing significant bets on a "super cycle" at this time. Key Levels: Not specified. Risks: Implied risk from being in a bear market; "super cycle" is presented as a speculative bet not currently favored. Sentiment: Bearish (Confidence: -0.7) Quote: "Are you going to go put it in in in crypto right now when it seems like crypto is in a bare market? I mean, maybe if you want to bet on the super cycle, but that's not where I'm placing a lot of my bets on." #### Palladium Thesis: Used as a historical example to illustrate chart patterns where major resistance levels (prior highs) are respected, and a breakout is often followed by a backtest and then a continued rally. Key Levels: Not specified for future investment. Referenced past rejection levels. Risks: Not discussed as a current investment recommendation. Sentiment: Neutral (Confidence: 0) Quote: "You see the major levels that palladium got rejected at on the way up are these like prior highs that it had, right?" #### Money Supply (M2) Thesis: The money supply (M2) is a critical macroeconomic factor. While a constant money supply is used for theoretical price calculations (e.g., gold/M2), the speaker asserts that the money supply "will not stay constant because they just can't help themselves." This implies ongoing fiat currency debasement, which is fundamentally bullish for gold. Key Levels: Not applicable. Risks: Not applicable, as it's a macroeconomic element. Sentiment: Bearish (for fiat currency, thus bullish for gold) (Confidence: 0.8) Quote: "The one thing we know is the money supply long-term will not stay constant because they just can't help themselves." #### Silver Thesis: Mentioned generally alongside gold as "metals" that have their time, implying it benefits from similar macroeconomic tailwinds. Key Levels: Not specified. Risks: Not elaborated upon. Sentiment: Neutral/Slightly Bullish (Confidence: 0.3) Quote: "It's easy to laugh at things like gold and silver, but there are times for them." ### Critique The speaker's logic relies heavily on technical analysis, specifically drawing parallels between gold's current chart patterns (gold/S&P, gold/M2) and historical breakouts observed in other assets like Bitcoin dominance, the HSI, and Palladium. While these historical patterns can offer valuable insights, a direct causal link between different asset classes based solely on visual chart similarities might oversimplify unique fundamental drivers. The argument that "the Fed printed our way out of it" in 2020 and is "not printing in the same way they were back then" is a crucial macroeconomic premise for gold's current strength, but the specifics of *how* current Fed policy differs and its direct impact on gold's valuation are not explicitly detailed. Regarding the $6,000 gold target, while it aligns with a long-term projection, the method for deriving the "another 20% rally" from the gold/M2 chart, which initially assumes a constant money supply (an assumption the speaker admits is unrealistic), could benefit from more robust quantitative explanation given the speaker's analytical role. The speaker does, however, provide a balanced view by acknowledging potential short-term pullbacks for gold both against the USD and the stock market. He also offers a critique of perpetual metal bulls, emphasizing the importance of recognizing macro turning points rather than blindly holding assets, stating: "you didn't have to sit on metals this entire time to get this upside. All you had to do was recognize that the macro was turning... and then you could have captured all these gains." This self-awareness regarding market timing and strategic allocation adds credibility to his overall thesis.

title: Tom Hayes - Schwab Network Appearance - 1/20/2026
analysis: ### Executive Summary The market outlook for 2026, a midterm election year, suggests a nuanced approach. While the S&P 500 historically sees muted returns (average 4.6%), with initial strength followed by pre-election weakness and a year-end recovery, the overarching theme is a shift in leadership from the Magnificent Seven (Mag Seven) to the broader market, dubbed the "un-magnificent 493." The speaker argues that the Mag Seven, now acting as "AI cost centers" due to massive CapEx investments, are experiencing decelerating earnings growth and impaired free cash flow, making them a "hard pass" for now. Conversely, "AI beneficiaries" – mainstream businesses leveraging AI to increase margins without the heavy CapEx – are poised for significant gains. This widening breadth, evidenced by nearly 70% of NYSE stocks above their 200-day moving average, signals a healthy market where fortunes will be made outside the highly weighted indices. Specific bullish picks include industrial cyclicals and energy companies, which benefit from an easing monetary cycle and increased demand, while trading at significantly lower multiples than tech giants. ### Asset Breakdown #### S&P 500 (Midterm Election Year) Thesis: Historically, midterm election years exhibit a distinct pattern: strong performance early in the year (through April), followed by weakness and uncertainty leading up to the election, and then a recovery into year-end. The average return since 1950 is 4.6%. Investors should "pick their spots." Key Levels: Not explicitly mentioned, but implies navigating volatility within the year. Risks: Historical weakness and uncertainty leading up to the midterm election. Catalysts: Initial market strength early in the year, subsequent recovery post-election. Sentiment: Neutral (with period-specific Bearish and Bullish phases), Confidence Score: 0.1 Quote: "If you go back to 1950, the average returns for the S&P 500 in a midterm election year are 4.6%. You tend to come out of the gate pretty strong. The market holds up through April, and then you get a lot of weakness into the uncertainty before the election and a recovery into year end." #### Magnificent Seven (Mag Seven) Thesis: These companies are seen as "AI cost centers" due to massive capital expenditure (CapEx) investments required for new technology. This is impairing their free cash flow, margins, and causing earnings deceleration (from 33% to low double digits). The return on invested capital will take "a little while" to materialize. Key Levels: Not mentioned. Risks: High CapEx, impaired free cash flow, compressed margins, decelerating earnings growth. Catalysts: Potential for bargains later in the year going into the election, as returns on investments might start showing "a year and a half, two years out." Sentiment: Bearish, Confidence Score: -0.8 Quote: "It's over 60% for Mag seven right now, which is actually right in line with the oil industry... Now they have to massively invest in this new technology and that's impairing their free cash flow. It's impairing their margins. And most importantly is earnings deceleration for the Mag seven." #### Un-Magnificent 493 (Rest of the Market) Thesis: This broader market segment represents "AI beneficiaries" – companies utilizing AI without the huge CapEx spend, leading to increased margins and lower costs. It exhibits widening breadth (69% of NYSE stocks above their 200-day moving average), accelerating earnings growth (from negative to low double digits), and significantly lower multiples compared to the Mag Seven. This segment is where "fortunes are going to be made in 2026." Key Levels: Not mentioned. Risks: Not explicitly mentioned, implied general market risks. Catalysts: Widening market breadth, accelerating earnings growth, lower valuations, benefits from "easing cycle" (industrial cyclicals). Sentiment: Bullish, Confidence Score: 0.9 Quote: "The UN magnificent for 93 the rest of the market went from negative earnings growth. Now is going to be back in low double digit earnings growth in coming quarters. The difference is the multiple for the rest of the market is so much lower than the Mag seven right now." #### Stanley Black & Decker (SWK) Thesis: An "everyday business" and an "AI beneficiary," Stanley Black & Decker has taken $2 billion of costs out of its business, improving margins from 33% (headed to 35%). The last time margins were 35%, the stock was $150; it is currently an $80 stock, suggesting it "could be a double." Key Levels: Current Price: ~$80. Take Profit: ~$150. Risks: Not explicitly mentioned, implied general business execution risks. Catalysts: Cost cutting, margin expansion due to AI utilization, historical valuation reversion. Time Horizon: "over the next 3 to 4 years." Sentiment: Bullish, Confidence Score: 0.9 Quote: "Their margins are back up to 33%, headed to 35%. The last time their margins were 35%, they earned over $8 a share and the stock was $150 stock. It's still today only an $80 stock, so this could be a double over the next 3 to 4 years." #### National Oilwell Varco (NOV) Thesis: A leader in onshore and offshore drilling rigs, NOV has $1 billion in free cash flow and $1 billion cash on its balance sheet. It will benefit from increased demand for energy driven by AI hyperscalers and data centers, as well as Venezuela coming back online. The energy sector, being at its lowest S&P weighting since 2020 (and 2000), historically signals a significant rebound. Key Levels: Not mentioned. Risks: Not explicitly mentioned, implied volatility within the energy sector. Catalysts: Increased energy demand (AI, data centers), Venezuela's return to market, historical undervaluation of the energy sector. Time Horizon: "over the next few years." Sentiment: Bullish, Confidence Score: 0.9 Quote: "They are going to benefit from the increased demand for energy for these AI, hyperscalers and data centers, etc. This is an industry you want to be in. They're also going to be a beneficiary over the next few years of increased demand from getting Venezuela back online." #### Energy Sector Thesis: The energy sector's weighting in the S&P 500 is at its lowest since 2020 and 2000. Historically, buying into the sector during such periods of low weighting and "flushed out" stocks has led to "fortunes" as they rebounded significantly.
